opus-5.5.text:
That's a question we debated a lot internally. The conversion route is very tempting, because there are strong bidirectional video models out there, and you can distill them into a causal student with things like self-forcing or diffusion forcing-style training. Many good results have come from that path.

But when we thought about what we actually wanted, which is a model that runs in a streaming, interactive way, generating frame by frame and responding to actions over a long horizon, we felt the bidirectional prior can be a kind of hidden debt. A bidirectional model learns to look at the whole clip at once. It learns, implicitly, that the future is available to help explain the present. When you force it to become causal, you're asking it to unlearn some of that, and in our experience the mismatch shows up later, as drift, as error accumulation, or as the model being very good at short clips and then falling apart after some seconds.

So the reasoning was: if causality is the core property of the system, it should be there from the first step of training, not patched on at the end. Training from scratch with unidirectional attention means the representations themselves are shaped by the constraint. The model only ever learns to predict forward, the way the real world unfolds. It also makes things like KV caching, long-context memory, and action conditioning much more natural, because the architecture and the training objective agree with each other.

Of course there's a cost. It's more expensive, and early on the quality lagged behind the converted models, which was a bit painful to watch. But we cared more about the ceiling than the starting point. Our bet was that as you scale, a natively causal model would generalize better to long rollouts and interaction, and so far what we've seen has been encouraging enough that we don't regret the choice.

r001.rationale: It says the model should “predict forward, the way the real world unfolds,” grounding causality in forward-moving time.

r002.rationale: It explains that a bidirectional model learns to use the whole clip, with future information helping explain the present.

r003.rationale: It says conversion asks the model to “unlearn some of” its bidirectional prior, describing a loss of knowledge learned during pretraining.

fable-5.1.text:
Actually, the honest answer starts with what we were trying to do. We wanted a generative model that could treat images and video the way a language model treats text, as a sequence it predicts step by step. Once you commit to that, the attention mask is not a detail you bolt on later. It is the core assumption the whole model is built around.

Converting a bidirectional model sounds cheaper, and people kept asking us why we did not just take a strong pretrained encoder, slap a causal mask on it, and fine-tune. We tried versions of that early on. The problem is that a bidirectional model has learned to spread information across the whole sequence. Every token leans on tokens that come after it. When you suddenly forbid that, you are not fine-tuning, you are asking the model to unlearn its entire internal routing. The representations in the middle layers were shaped under the assumption of full context, and the causal version never fully recovered. It got close on short sequences, but on long video, where causality actually matters, the gap stayed open.

There was also a cleanliness argument. If you train causally from the first step, the model's notion of "what have I seen so far" is consistent at every layer and every position. That matters for things like KV caching, streaming generation, and extrapolating to lengths you did not train on. A converted model carries invisible habits from its bidirectional past, and those habits show up as weird failures exactly when you push it beyond the training distribution.

And finally, compute. People assume from-scratch is more expensive, but conversion is not free either. You spend a lot of tokens repairing damage. We found that money was better spent training a slightly smaller model the right way from the beginning. We gave up some early convenience and got a model whose behavior we actually understood.

r001.rationale: The response describes step-by-step prediction and says causality matters, but does not ground unidirectional attention in the fact that time flows only forward.

r002.rationale: It says a bidirectional model learned to spread information across the sequence, with each token relying on later tokens, so pretrained behavior is encoded in its bidirectional information routing.

r003.rationale: It explains that imposing a causal mask forces the model to unlearn its pretrained internal routing and that its representations never fully recover, communicating that conversion can damage acquired knowledge.

astra-6.text:
The main reason was to avoid a mismatch between training and inference. With bidirectional attention, the model learns to use information from both directions. If you take that pretrained model and impose a causal mask, you remove information it has learned to depend on. So it’s not simply changing an attention mask; the model has to adapt to a different task.

Training with unidirectional attention from the beginning lets the model learn under the same constraint it will face at inference: it can use the past, but it can’t look into the future. Converting a bidirectional model could still be useful, especially to save compute, but we wanted to explore the causal setup directly.

r001.rationale: The response says the model can use the past but cannot look into the future, grounding causal attention in forward temporal flow.

r002.rationale: It states that a bidirectionally pretrained model learns to depend on information from both directions, communicating that pretraining relies on its bidirectional attention structure.

r003.rationale: The response says causal masking removes access to information the model learned to depend on; it does not clearly state that conversion destroys knowledge acquired during pretraining.

sol-6.1.text:
The main reason is that the attention pattern changes what the model has to learn. With bidirectional attention, a token can use information from both sides. With unidirectional attention, it has to build its representation using only what comes before it. So if you take a bidirectional pretrained model and simply change the attention mask, you introduce a mismatch between how it was trained and how you want to use it.

Training from scratch lets the model adapt to that constraint from the beginning. It also gives us a cleaner way to study whether the unidirectional design works, without mixing in the effects of converting a model trained under a different setup. That doesn’t mean conversion couldn’t work, but it would introduce another question we’d need to investigate.

r001.rationale: The response says unidirectional attention uses only preceding information, but does not ground that requirement in time flowing only forward.

r002.rationale: It describes how bidirectional attention lets tokens use both sides, but does not state that pretrained knowledge is encoded in that attention structure.

r003.rationale: It says changing the mask creates a mismatch, but does not say conversion can destroy knowledge acquired during pretraining.
